'''''Euphorbia nivulia''''' is a subtropical [[succulent plant|succulent]] [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Euphorbiaceae]]. It is found in the Indian subcontinent and is commonly known as the '''leafy milk hedge''', '''holy milk hedge''' or '''dog's tongue'''.<ref name=FlowersofIndia>{{cite web |url=https://www.flowersofindia.net/catalog/slides/Leafy%20Milk%20Hedge.html |title=Leafy milk hedge |publisher=Flowers of India |access-date=2 October 2021}}</ref>

==Description==
''Euphorbia nivulia'' forms a small tree up to {{convert|9|m|ft|0|abbr=on}} high and {{convert|1|m|ft|0|abbr=on}} in girth. The bark is rough and thick. The branches are succulent, and grow out from the trunk at an obtuse angle. Spirally arranged tubercles on the branches bear clusters of sharp spines. The leaves are simple and arranged alternately, and have a very short or no stalk. The leaf blade is obovate and spoon-shaped to inverted-lance-shaped, up to {{convert|25|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|8|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} wide. They are thick and fleshy, the tip is rounded, the base is tapered, and the margin is entire. The midrib is prominent on the underside of the leaf. The reddish [[Cyathium|cyathia]] (false flowers found in the genus ''[[Euphorbia]]'') develop in groups of three in the axils of the leaves towards the ends of the branches. The fruits are divided into three parts, the lobes being compressed laterally. The seeds are four-angled and ovoid, smooth and about {{convert|4|mm|in|2|abbr=on}} long.<ref name=FlowersofIndia/> This plant is similar to ''[[Euphorbia caducifolia]]'', leafless milk hedge, but it retains its leaves for longer than does ''E. caducifolia'', and does not form bushy thickets.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.flowersofindia.net/catalog/slides/Leafless%20Milk%20Hedge.html |title=Leafless milk hedge |publisher=Flowers of India |access-date=3 October 2021}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Euphorbia nivulia'' is native to Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Myanmar.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:347506-1 |title=''Euphorbia nivulia'' Buch.-Ham. |publisher=Plants of the World Online |access-date=2 October 2021}}</ref> It grows in both wet and dry deciduous forests on rocky hillsides,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://indiabiodiversity.org/species/show/229703 |title=''Euphorbia nivulia'' Buch.-Ham. |publisher=India Biodiversity Portal |access-date=2 October 2021}}</ref> and also in dry, barren areas; it is planted as a hedge plant in agricultural areas.<ref name=Mahajan>{{cite journal |author1=Mahajan, Raghunath T. |author2=Badgujar, Shamkant B. |name-list-style=amp |year=2011 |title=Bioprospecting of ''Euphorbia nivulia'' Buch.-Ham. |journal=International Journal of Phytopharmacology |volume=2 |issue=2 |pages=37–42 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/260256905 }}</ref>

==Uses==
Juice squeezed from the leaves, bark from the root, the stems and the latex have been used in traditional medicine. Research has shown that the plant possesses  antimicrobial, wound healing, haemostatic and cytotoxic activity. Additionally, it possesses larvicidal, insecticidal and nematicidal activities, and may prove useful in controlling the mosquitoes, ''[[Aedes aegypti]]'' and ''[[Culex quinquefasciatus]]'', and suppressing the [[root-knot nematode]], (''Meloidogyne incognita'').<ref name=Mahajan/>
